strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of video-to-audio generation: semantic and temporal alignment alone do not establish that acoustic responses reflect interaction dynamics. Combining object-level physical estimates with a general-purpose audio generator is potentially useful.

Table 1 shows substantial improvements over MMAudio-L in FD-PaSST (60.60 to 47.38), FD-PANNs (4.72 to 3.99), and ImageBind score (33.22 to 35.41). These results support the practical value of the proposed conditioning pipeline, although improvements are not universal.

Table 3 includes a useful longer-training control and comparisons of mass conditioning, velocity conditioning, and injection strategies. The combined model achieves the best distributional fidelity and inception score among these configurations.

VGG-Impact provides a focused evaluation setting, and the 15-participant study offers complementary perceptual evidence: reported physical-plausibility ratings improve from 3.96 to 4.34 over MMAudio-L.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate physical information from additional object-centric visual conditioning. Both mass and velocity branches also introduce masked CLIP features and extra conditioning capacity. Table 3 lacks an otherwise identical object-feature-only adapter or shuffled/constant physical-value controls, and reports no APCC ablations. Consequently, it does not establish that meaningful mass and velocity estimates cause the gains rather than richer visual features.

APCC has insufficient validation as a measure of physical realism. A single object's translational kinetic-energy decrease need not equal energy dissipated by the interaction, and only a variable fraction becomes recorded sound. Material, rotation, energy transfer, microphone distance, and recording gain complicate the relationship with spectral onset strength. Comparing against real-audio correlations is helpful, but class-level correlation agreement can still coexist with incorrect individual impact sounds. Raw ground-truth correlations, per-class results, uncertainty, and agreement with human judgments are not reported.

The reliability of the physical estimates is asserted rather than demonstrated in the supplied manuscript. Section 4.2 refers all estimator results to supplementary material that is not included. In particular, Eq. (3) differentiates centroids of visible reconstructed surfaces, which can move because of occlusion, rotation, or reconstruction noise rather than object translation. The manuscript provides no quantitative evidence establishing reliable metric scale or impact-time velocities, despite using these estimates for both conditioning and evaluation.

Important evaluation details are missing. APCC lacks a precise mathematical definition and specifies neither onset matching across generated and reference audio nor treatment of missing or spurious impacts, object assignment, or class aggregation. VGG-Impact contains 272 moments across ten classes, but class counts and clip counts are absent. The user study does not clearly establish the number of evaluated clips, assignment protocol, or statistical uncertainty of paired improvements; its caption also describes eight generated audios while listing seven methods.

Reproducibility and practical cost remain incompletely characterized: VLM configuration and prompts, several adapter settings, and benchmark construction details are deferred outside the supplied document, while end-to-end runtime and memory costs of the estimation pipeline are unreported. Overall, the generation gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved attribution and validation issues concern the central physics-aware contribution and currently outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile limitation of video-to-audio synthesis: semantic agreement and synchronization do not establish that sound intensity reflects visible interaction dynamics. Object-level mass and motion conditioning is a relevant direction for audiovisual generation.

Table 1 provides substantive evidence of improved generation over the strong MMAudio-L baseline: FD-PaSST decreases from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, and ImageBind alignment increases from 33.22 to 35.41. These improvements support the practical usefulness of the proposed conditioning pipeline.

The adapter is technically coherent, combining object-masked visual features, scalar embeddings, FiLM, and residual AdaLN modulation. Table 3 includes a useful longer-training control and demonstrates benefits from both conditioning branches beyond additional backbone training.

VGG-Impact and APCC attempt to evaluate an overlooked property. PAVAS improves APCC-Δ from 0.536 to 0.378, and the 15-participant study reports higher physical-plausibility ratings than MMAudio-L, providing encouraging complementary evidence.
weaknesses: The main causal claim is not isolated by the ablations. Both physics branches introduce object-centric CLIP features and additional trainable conditioning capacity alongside mass or velocity. Table 3 lacks an otherwise identical object-feature-only adapter, constant/shuffled physical inputs, or a simpler motion-cue control. It also omits APCC. Consequently, the results establish that the augmented architecture helps, but do not establish that meaningful physical quantities drive the gains. The conclusion that improvements exceed what visual features alone offer is insufficiently supported.

APCC is not adequately validated as a measure of physical realism. Translational kinetic-energy loss of one object is not generally the energy radiated acoustically: energy can transfer to another object, rotation, deformation, or heat, while recording distance and gain affect measured onset strength. Comparing with ground-truth correlation is a useful precaution, but matching a class-level correlation does not establish correct event-level acoustics. Since the metric also uses the estimator that supplies model conditioning, independent physical measurements or validation against human judgments are particularly important.

The reliability of the physical inputs remains unsupported in the supplied manuscript. Section 4.2 asserts favorable estimator accuracy but defers all numerical results and protocols to supplementary material that is not included. VLM-inferred mass can reflect category priors rather than actual object mass, and changes in the centroid of visible reconstructed points can reflect occlusion or viewpoint changes rather than true motion. Centroid speed also misses rotational impacts. These limitations directly affect both conditioning and the proposed evaluation.

The central physical evaluation is insufficiently specified and its uncertainty is unreported. VGG-Impact contains 272 impact moments across 10 classes, but the manuscript does not provide per-class counts, ground-truth correlations, confidence intervals, an explicit APCC-Δ aggregation formula, or rules for matching missing, extra, or shifted generated onsets to visual impacts. The user study likewise leaves the number of evaluated clips and randomization protocol unclear. These omissions make the magnitude and robustness of the physical-consistency improvement difficult to assess.

The architectural novelty is primarily the application and integration of established components, so convincing attribution and physical validation are especially important. Reproducibility is also limited by missing estimator prompts, model configurations, and several adapter details in the supplied document. Separately, the broad performance language should acknowledge regressions against MMAudio-L in FD-VGG (0.97 to 1.15) and DeSync (0.442 to 0.446). These presentation issues are secondary: the recommendation is driven by the unresolved evidence for physical grounding, despite credible general audio-generation gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful audiovisual generation problem: matching sound intensity and dynamics to visible object interactions. Extending physical conditioning to diverse, unconstrained videos is potentially useful beyond narrowly controlled impact-sound settings.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and reasonably well explained. Object-centric features, separate mass and velocity modulation, and residual injection into the diffusion backbone provide a practical integration of physical estimates with a strong generative model.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements over MMAudio-L on several metrics: FD-PaSST decreases from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, and ImageBind alignment increases from 33.22 to 35.41. APCC-∆ also improves from 0.536 to 0.378. These results support the utility of the overall system, although improvements are not universal.

Table 3 includes a useful longer-training control and separate mass, velocity, and injection-strategy ablations. The full configuration improves distributional quality and inception score over the backbone, while the 15-participant study provides additional, directionally consistent perceptual evidence.
weaknesses: The central attribution to physical quantities remains unresolved. The adapter introduces object masks, object-centric CLIP features, and additional conditioning capacity alongside mass and velocity. Table 3 lacks an otherwise identical object-feature-only adapter or shuffled/constant-physics controls, and reports no APCC ablations. Consequently, it does not establish that meaningful physical values, rather than richer visual conditioning, cause the gains.

APCC is insufficiently validated as a measure of physical realism. It uses predicted physical quantities from the same estimation pipeline that supplies model conditioning, so agreement can reflect consistency with estimator biases. Moreover, one object's translational kinetic-energy loss is not generally the acoustic energy released: energy transfer, rotation, deformation, material, and recording conditions matter. Comparing against real-audio correlations is sensible, but the manuscript provides neither those classwise correlations nor uncertainty estimates or independent validation against physical-plausibility judgments.

The claimed reliability of PPE is not supported by results in the supplied manuscript. Comparisons with specialist mass and velocity estimators are deferred to supplementary material that is not included. Learned monocular metric reconstruction and VLM mass priors can be useful, but visible-surface centroid differences are also sensitive to occlusion, rotation, segmentation changes, and reconstruction drift. Without quantitative validation, the claims of reliable metric velocity and mass remain unsubstantiated.

Important evaluation and reproduction details are missing. APCC-∆ lacks an explicit mathematical definition, class aggregation rule, impact-window specification, and treatment of missing or extra generated onsets. VGG-Impact contains 272 events across 10 classes, but classwise sample counts and statistical uncertainty are absent. The human-study description does not clearly specify the number of evaluated clips, randomization, or instructions for distinguishing physical plausibility from general audiovisual alignment.

The architectural originality is primarily in integrating existing estimators and standard Fourier, FiLM, and AdaLN mechanisms. That integration can merit acceptance, but its distinctive physics-related benefit needs stronger isolation than the current evidence provides. Overall, the demonstrated generation gains are worthwhile; the unresolved attribution and validation of the central physical-grounding claim place the balance at weak reject.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of video-to-audio synthesis: semantic and temporal alignment do not necessarily imply plausible responses to physical interactions. Combining object-level mass and motion estimates with a generative audio backbone is potentially useful.

PAVAS shows meaningful improvements over the strong MMAudio-L baseline. Table 1 reports FDPaSST improving from 60.60 to 47.38, FDPANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, and ImageBind score from 33.22 to 35.41. Table S6 also demonstrates benefits outside impact-related classes.

The conditioning architecture is technically plausible. Object-centric features, bounded FiLM modulation, and zero-initialized residual AdaLN corrections provide a coherent integration of estimated physical cues. Table 3 includes useful controls for additional training, individual conditioning streams, and injection strategy.

The supplement provides substantial implementation and diagnostic detail, including VLM prompts, checkpoints, training settings, runtime, missing-observation statistics, estimator evaluations, and perturbation/fallback experiments. These improve reproducibility and acknowledge practical pipeline limitations.
The user study provides complementary evidence: 27 participants favor PAVAS across all four dimensions, including physical plausibility increasing from 3.90 to 4.37 relative to MMAudio-L.
weaknesses: The central physics metric cannot establish important parts of the claimed contribution. Section D.2 z-normalizes energy changes within each video before computing class correlations. For a fixed tracked object, mass is a positive constant multiplying every energy change and therefore cancels under this normalization. Uniform rescaling of that object's velocity also cancels. Consequently, APCC cannot validate mass-dependent acoustic scaling or absolute metric calibration in this common setting, despite being presented as evidence for both mass and velocity grounding.

APCC also has unresolved event-selection and validation issues. Onsets are detected separately from each generated waveform, so different models can be evaluated at different physical times and on different event sets. Missing or extra impacts and object-to-onset association are not adequately specified. Matching a class-level correlation does not ensure correct event-level sound strength. The 272-event benchmark lacks per-class ground-truth correlations, sample counts, and uncertainty estimates; shuffling and noise tests alone do not establish agreement with human judgments of physical realism.

The ablations do not isolate physical values from the additional object-centric visual pathway. Both mass and velocity streams contain masked CLIP features, but Table 3 lacks a matched adapter using those features with constant or shuffled physical inputs. It also omits APCC results for its component ablations. Thus, the reported gains could partly reflect better object localization or additional conditioning capacity. Inference-time perturbations demonstrate sensitivity to inputs but do not resolve this attribution problem.

The physical interpretation of the estimated energy remains insufficiently supported. Velocities use unsmoothed differences of visible-point centroids at only 8 FPS, which can miss rapid impact dynamics and vary with changing visible surfaces. STARSS23 evaluates a displacement proxy on manually filtered tracks, rather than pre/post-impact velocity accuracy. Moreover, one object's translational kinetic-energy loss need not equal dissipated collision energy because energy can transfer to another object or into rotation and deformation. These issues matter for the benchmark's door, hammer, and pool interactions.

The subjective evidence is encouraging but covers only eight selected clips, and the reported standard deviations do not quantify uncertainty across clips. Some broad performance claims also exceed the results: PAVAS-L worsens FDVGG and slightly worsens DeSync versus MMAudio-L, while impact-set IS decreases. These are limitations of the claimed consistency, not reasons to require universal benchmark superiority.

Overall, the practical generation gains are worthwhile, but the recommendation favors rejection because the main scientific claim—improved physical grounding specifically attributable to mass and velocity—is not adequately separated from object-centric visual conditioning, and its principal evaluation has consequential validity limitations. These concerns outweigh presentation refinements or limited evaluation breadth alone.

strengths: PAVAS addresses a meaningful limitation of video-to-audio synthesis: whether acoustic responses reflect visible interaction dynamics. Combining object-level physical estimates with a general audio generator is potentially useful beyond narrowly constrained impact-sound systems.

The main results demonstrate substantial practical gains over MMAudio-L: FD-PaSST improves from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, and ImageBind alignment from 33.22 to 35.41 (Table 1). Supplementary Table S6 reports improvements on both impact and non-impact subsets.

The adapter design is technically plausible, combining object features, scalar conditioning, FiLM, and residual AdaLN modulation. Table 3 includes a useful longer-training control and shows benefits from both conditioning streams and their combination.

The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, including VLM prompts, model checkpoints, training settings, missing-observation handling, and runtime measurements. Estimator evaluations, perturbation experiments, and fallback tests provide useful evidence about the pipeline's behavior.

The user study favors PAVAS across all four criteria, including physical plausibility (4.37 versus 3.90 for MMAudio-L). This provides perceptual support independent of the proposed automatic metric, although its scene coverage is limited.
weaknesses: The ablations do not isolate physical values from the additional object-centric visual information. Both mass and velocity streams contain masked CLIP features, whereas the backbone lacks this pathway. Table 3 therefore cannot establish that its gains specifically require meaningful mass and velocity estimates. An otherwise identical object-feature adapter with constant or shuffled physical values is missing. Inference-time perturbations establish sensitivity, but do not resolve this training-time confound; Table 3 also omits APCC.

APCC has a consequential limitation for evaluating the central mass-conditioning claim. Supplement D.2 normalizes energy changes within each video before correlation. For events involving one object with constant mass, the multiplicative mass term cancels exactly under this normalization; uniform velocity scaling likewise cancels. The metric can assess relative event variation, but cannot validate absolute physical magnitudes or mass-dependent acoustic scaling in these cases. Using the same PPE estimates for conditioning and evaluation further limits its independence.

The APCC event protocol is insufficiently specified and potentially model-dependent. Onsets are extracted separately from generated audio, so different systems can be evaluated at different physical times and on different event sets. Missing or additional impacts, object assignment, insufficient-event clips, and the pre-onset neighborhood are not clearly resolved. With only 272 impact moments across ten classes, the absence of per-class correlations and uncertainty estimates makes the 0.536-to-0.378 improvement difficult to interpret. Shuffling and noise tests do not establish agreement with human judgments of physical plausibility.

The physical estimator validation does not establish accuracy at impact times. Velocity is obtained from unsmoothed visible-surface centroid differences at 8 FPS, which can be affected by changing visibility and can miss rapid pre/post-impact dynamics. The STARSS23 evaluation uses manually filtered masks and a displacement proxy rather than impact-velocity ground truth. Moreover, translational centroid energy alone does not capture rotational or articulated interactions such as door closing and hammering. These limitations weaken the interpretation of the estimated energy drop as physically grounded impact energy.

The perceptual evidence is encouraging but narrower than the manuscript's broad claims. The user study covers only eight clips, and reported standard deviations do not establish uncertainty across scenes. Table 1 also shows worse FD-VGG and slightly worse DeSync than MMAudio-L. These are qualifications rather than rejection grounds by themselves; the recommendation is driven primarily by the unresolved attribution of gains to physical conditioning and the limited validity of the central physics evaluation.

strengths: PAVAS addresses a meaningful limitation of video-to-audio synthesis: matching sound intensity and dynamics to visible physical interactions. Object-level mass and motion conditioning provides a useful, interpretable extension beyond semantic and temporal alignment.

The empirical improvements over the strong MMAudio-L baseline are substantial on several measures: FD-PaSST improves from 60.60 to 47.38, FD-PANNs from 4.72 to 3.99, and ImageBind score from 33.22 to 35.41. Supplementary results show benefits on both impact and non-impact videos.

Table 3 includes a valuable additional-training control. Combining mass and velocity improves FD-PaSST from 70.19 to 65.67 and IS from 14.44 to 16.50, whereas simply training the backbone longer does not help. Residual modulation also outperforms direct summation.

The evaluation includes estimator benchmarks, perturbation experiments, missing-cue fallback tests, runtime profiling, and human judgments. The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, including model checkpoints, VLM prompts, preprocessing, and training settings.
weaknesses: The central attribution to physical quantities remains incomplete. Both conditioning branches introduce additional object-centric visual features, but Table 3 lacks an otherwise identical adapter using those features with constant or shuffled physical values. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly separated from improved object localization and added conditioning capacity. The component ablations also omit APCC.

APCC has an important limitation for evaluating mass awareness. Section D.2 normalizes energy changes separately within each video; when events involve one fixed-mass object, its positive mass factor cancels exactly under this normalization. The metric therefore cannot establish whether the model captures mass-dependent acoustic scaling in this common case. Correlation matching also does not establish correct absolute acoustic magnitude.

APCC uses each generated waveform's detected onsets to select the corresponding physical measurements, potentially evaluating different events for different methods. Event matching, missed or extra onsets, single-event clips, and multi-object assignment are insufficiently specified. Using the same PPE for conditioning and evaluation further limits independent validation; shuffling and noise tests do not resolve these concerns.

The physical interpretation of the estimated energy drop is stronger than the evidence supports. Unsmooth centroid differences at 8 FPS need not capture pre/post-impact velocities, and the nearest onset frame is not necessarily post-impact. Translational energy lost by one object can transfer to other objects, rotation, or deformation. The filtered STARSS23 displacement evaluation is useful but does not validate impact-energy estimates on VGG-Impact.

The independent evidence for physical plausibility remains limited: VGG-Impact contains 272 selected moments with no per-class correlations or uncertainty estimates, and the human study covers only eight clips despite having 27 participants. PAVAS also slightly worsens DeSync and FD-VGG relative to MMAudio-L. Overall, the demonstrated synthesis gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved attribution and physical-evaluation issues place the submission at the acceptance boundary.
